hints: Focus on the N atom only, and count how many atoms it is bonded to and how many lone pairs it still holds.
Notice N forms a single bond to $\text{CH}_3$ and a double bond to C, leaving one lone pair, so there are 3 electron regions in total.
Recall what bond angle goes with 3 regions and one lone pair, a bent shape based on trigonal planar geometry.
walkthrough:
**Draw what is around the N atom**

Look closely at the structure $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{N}=\text{C}=\text{O}$. The N atom makes two bonding connections, one single bond to $\text{CH}_3$ and one double bond to C.

Bonding domains on N = 2

**Find the lone pair on N**

Nitrogen is in Group 15, so it has 5 outer electrons. It uses 3 electrons in bonding (1 for the single bond, 2 for the double bond), leaving 2 electrons as one lone pair.

$$\text{electron regions on N} = 2 \text{ bonding} + 1 \text{ lone pair} = 3$$

**Use VSEPR to get the angle**

Three electron regions gives a trigonal planar electron arrangement. With one lone pair, the molecular shape at N is bent.

The basic trigonal planar angle is $120^{\circ}$, and the lone pair squeezes it only slightly, so the approximate angle is $120^{\circ}$.

options.A: 104 degrees is the bent angle for 4 electron regions with 2 lone pairs, like in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. N here has only 3 regions with 1 lone pair, not 4 regions.
options.B: 109 degrees is the tetrahedral angle for 4 electron regions, like in $\text{CH}_4$ or $\text{NH}_3$. N in $\text{CH}_3\text{NCO}$ has only 3 regions, so this does not apply.
options.C: Correct. N has 2 bonding domains plus 1 lone pair, giving 3 electron regions with trigonal planar arrangement. The $\text{C}-\text{N}=\text{C}$ angle is therefore approximately 120 degrees.
options.D: 180 degrees would mean a linear arrangement with 2 electron regions and no lone pair on N, like the C atom in $\text{N}=\text{C}=\text{O}$. It ignores the lone pair on N which bends the bonds.
